planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Prague tolerates colder winters than standard mandarins thanks to its trifoliate orange parentage.

directions: Prague is one of a small group of citrandarins USDA breeders produced by crossing cold-hardy trifoliate orange with mandarin to push edible citrus further north than pure mandarins can survive. The small, tart, seedy fruit is more useful for juice, ade, or marmalade than fresh peeling, and the tree carries the trifoliate parent's semi-deciduous habit and light thorns. Grow it as a curiosity for pushing the cold edge of dooryard citrus in the Gulf South, siting it in a warm microclimate and protecting young trees for their first few winters. Established trees tolerate hard freezes that would kill a standard orange or mandarin outright.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sinton is among the most cold-hardy of the historic citrangequats, tolerating winters that would kill standard citrus.

directions: Sinton was bred alongside the better-known Thomasville and Telfair citrangequats in the early 1900s by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle, crossing cold-hardy citrange (trifoliate orange x sweet orange) with kumquat to create an edible-skinned, tart-sweet novelty citrus for the coldest edge of the citrus range. Small, rounded, orange fruit has an aromatic marmalade-type flavor best suited to preserves and candying rather than fresh eating. The tree is a compact, thorny large shrub well suited to Gulf Coast hobbyist plantings where standard citrus struggles to survive hard freezes. Give it full sun, good drainage, and winter protection for young trees to get established.

common_name: Kiyomi Tangor (Satsuma-Orange Hybrid, Parent of Sumo Citrus)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; protect young trees from freezes, since Kiyomi is less cold-hardy than Satsuma mandarins.

directions: Kiyomi is a Japanese-bred tangor, a cross of Satsuma mandarin and Trovita sweet orange developed at the Okitsu citrus research station, prized for exceptionally sweet, low-acid, richly aromatic juice with a deep orange rind and few seeds when grown in isolation from other citrus. It is best known as the parent of Dekopon/Sumo Citrus, but the fruit stands on its own merits for home orchardists wanting a specialty dessert citrus distinct from the more common Satsumas and navels already in wide cultivation. Kiyomi needs more heat and a longer frost-free season than Satsuma mandarins, so it suits warmer zone 9-11 gardens and container culture further north. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily, since Kiyomi can overbear and produce undersized fruit the following year.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: W. Murcott Afourer Mandarin (Late-Season Seedy Parent of Tango Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; fruit stays seedless only if no other citrus blooms nearby, since Afourer readily cross-pollinates.

directions: Afourer, marketed in the US as W. Murcott, is a late-winter Moroccan-origin mandarin valued for deep orange color, intensely sweet flavor, and easy-peel skin, ripening after most other mandarins have finished. Unlike its seedless sport Tango, Afourer readily develops seeds when planted near other citrus, so growers wanting guaranteed seedless fruit should isolate it or choose Tango instead; those without nearby citrus can grow Afourer itself for a slightly richer, more complex flavor some tasters prefer. It is a vigorous, productive tree that bears heavily once established and benefits from fruit thinning in on years. Water deeply but infrequently and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for best fruit quality.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, ideally within 50 feet of pollination-variant persimmon cultivars that need a pollen source.

directions: Gailey is grown less for its own small, seedy fruit than for the abundant male flowers it produces, making it the standard pollinator variety planted alongside pollination-variant Asian persimmons such as Chocolate and other PVA/PVNA types that only develop their best flavor, texture, and dark flesh color when fertilized. One Gailey tree can supply pollen for several seed-dependent persimmons within about 50 feet, letting a home orchard grow a wider range of specialty non-astringent persimmons than seedless cultivars alone would allow. The tree itself is tough, low-maintenance, and drought-tolerant once established, needing little beyond routine pruning to keep it manageable near the trees it pollinates. Because most persimmon cultivars in trade are self-fruitful, Gailey is a specialty planting for gardeners specifically chasing pollination-variant fruit quality rather than a first persimmon tree.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Wabash American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, setting young trees carefully to avoid disturbing the long taproot.

directions: Wabash is a historic Midwestern selection of native American persimmon valued for its large fruit size relative to wild trees and its vigorous, dependable growth. Orange-fleshed fruit ripens in fall and turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich once fully soft, but stays mouth-puckeringly astringent if eaten too early, so wait until fruit yields to gentle pressure or drops naturally. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established, and its deep taproot makes it a long-lived, low-maintenance choice for food-forest or wildlife plantings. Provide a second genetically distinct native persimmon nearby for best fruit set unless a known self-fertile selection is planted, and remove root suckers regularly to keep it from forming a thicket.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: Claypool American Persimmon (Productive Midwestern Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding root disturbance to the long taproot.

directions: Claypool is an old Indiana-origin named selection of native American persimmon recognized for heavy, reliable annual production and good fruit size compared to typical seedling trees found in the wild. Fruit ripens in fall to a deep orange, soft, jelly-like texture with rich, honeyed sweetness once fully ripe, but remains harshly astringent while firm, so let fruit soften fully or wait for it to drop before eating. As with most native persimmons, Claypool grows a deep taproot and tolerates heat, drought, and marginal soils far better than typical orchard fruit trees once established, making it well suited to low-input food-forest plantings. Plant a second, genetically distinct persimmon cultivar nearby for pollination and heavier fruit set, and thin root suckers to keep the tree from spreading into a thicket.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Evelyn ripens ahead of most native persimmon selections, useful where hard fall frosts arrive early.

directions: Evelyn is a named native persimmon selection prized chiefly for ripening its crop earlier than most American persimmon cultivars, letting growers in shorter-season areas harvest a full crop of soft, sweet fruit before hard frost cuts the season short. Fruit is medium-sized and richly sweet once fully soft-ripe, but like all American persimmons is intensely astringent while firm and must be left to ripen fully on the tree or after dropping. The tree shares the species' deep taproot, drought tolerance, and adaptability to poor or marginal soils, asking little beyond routine watering while young and occasional sucker removal. Pair Evelyn with a second, genetically distinct persimmon selection nearby to improve pollination and fruit set.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
